A_target.statement:
Let $X$ be a [[Definition:Continuous Random Variable|continuous random variable]] with [[Definition:Probability Density Function|probability density function]] $f_X$.
Then:
:$\displaystyle \expect X = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x \map {f_X} x \rd x$
and if $\tuple {X, Y}$ has joint density $f_{X, Y}$, the [[Definition:Marginal Distribution|marginal]] density of $X$ is:
:$\displaystyle \map {f_X} x = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \map {f_{X, Y} } {x, y} \rd y$

B_source.statement:
Let $X$ be a [[Definition:Discrete Random Variable|discrete random variable]] with [[Definition:Probability Mass Function|probability mass function]] $p_X$.
Then:
:$\displaystyle \expect X = \sum_x x \map {p_X} x$
and the [[Definition:Marginal Distribution|marginal]] mass function of $X$ is:
:$\displaystyle \map {p_X} x = \sum_y \map {p_{X, Y} } {x, y}$

substitutions.the probability of a single outcome: the density value, which is not itself a probability

derived.the expectation formula: the same formula with the sum replaced by an integral
derived.conditioning on an outcome: conditioning on a measure-zero event, which needs a limiting definition

validity_conditions: Sums and integrals are both integration against a measure, counting measure in one case and Lebesgue measure in the other, so every formula linear in the mass function transfers.
Individual points have probability zero in the continuous case, so a density value is not a probability and may exceed one; statements about the probability of a single outcome do not transfer.

Conditioning on the value of a continuous variable conditions on a null event and is not defined by the elementary ratio; it requires conditional densities or the general theory, and naive transfer produces the Borel-Kolmogorov paradox.
proof_plan: Replace the [[Definition:Probability Mass Function|mass function]] $p_X$ by the [[Definition:Probability Density Function|density]] $f_X$, and summation by [[Definition:Lebesgue Integral|integration]].

Statements about individual outcomes do not transfer.
For a continuous random variable, $\map \Pr {X = x} = 0$ for all $x$, and $\map {f_X} x$ is not a probability.

Conditioning on $\set {X = x}$ cannot be defined as the elementary ratio $\dfrac {\map \Pr {A \cap B} } {\map \Pr B}$.
Define instead the [[Definition:Conditional Probability Density Function|conditional density]]:
:$\map {f_{Y \mid X} } {y \mid x} = \dfrac {\map {f_{X, Y} } {x, y} } {\map {f_X} x}$
{{qed}}
